extracted.intended_audience: patent scholars, practitioners, law students, and policymakers interested in patentable subject matter and empirical patent-law research
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing how predictable the Alice/Mayo patent-eligibility doctrine is in practice using empirical indicators from Federal Circuit decisions (affirmance, dissent, and error rates) and methodological practices (datasets, coding, transparency).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo test (directed-to + inventive concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the 'Alice/Mayo' test, if a patent claim is 'directed to' an ineligible concept (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas), it is patentable only if it also contains an 'inventive concept' such that the claim 'amounts to significantly more' than a patent on the ineligible concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the doctrinal standard for patentable subject matter that analysts and courts apply; disputes about applying the two-step framework to borderline claims are a core source of perceived unpredictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmance rate as a predictability metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal/affirmance rates measure how often an appeals court affirms lower-tribunal decisions; the authors found the Federal Circuit affirmed lower tribunals almost 90% of the time (over 95% for USPTO appeals; ~85% for district-court appeals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High affirmance rates are used as evidence that a doctrine is being applied consistently in practice; compare affirmance rates for eligibility to other doctrines to contextualize predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissent rate as a predictability/uniformity metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissent rates indicate how frequently judges publicly disagree; eligibility decisions had fewer dissents than other patent-law issues (6.5% vs. 8.1% overall; 8.6% vs. 10.7% for district-court appeals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower dissent rates suggest greater unanimity and therefore greater doctrinal uniformity; use dissent frequency as a complement to affirmance/reversal metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error rate (identification of legal error even when affirming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an appeals court identifies a legal error in a lower tribunal's analysis even while affirming the result; in the study, three coders reviewed 153 affirming opinions (excluding Rule 36) and found errors in only seven opinions (<5%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Error rates indicate whether courts are reaching correct results for the right reasons; a low error rate supports the claim that the law can be predictably applied, and can serve as a benchmark for future empirical comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 36 summary affirmances frequency and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit frequently and asymmetrically used Rule 36 summary affirmances in patent-eligibility cases; the dataset included a large number of these summary affirmances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 36 entries lack full opinions and reasoning, which can obscure doctrinal development and affect empirical measures of predictability; analyses should account for the prevalence and impact of Rule 36 dispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source-of-appeal composition and selection bias (USPTO vs district courts)
rubrics_metrics.description: About one-quarter of eligibility appeals came from the USPTO and three-quarters from district courts; only ineligibility decisions are appealed from the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The origin of appeals creates selection effects (e.g., USPTO appeals are skewed toward ineligibility rulings), so researchers must stratify or control for source when using affirmance/reversal statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural posture and standard of review (deference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many district-court eligibility appeals were decided in procedural postures in which the district court receives no deference, yet the Federal Circuit still affirmed a high percentage of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High affirmance despite non-deferential review strengthens claims of predictability; analysts should note standard-of-review differences when interpreting affirmance rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of eligibility as a litigation shortcut (case-selection effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility may be used largely as a 'shortcut' to quickly dispose of clearly invalid patents early in litigation (e.g., at the pleadings stage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If eligibility is concentrated in easier-to-decide cases, observed predictability may reflect case-selection rather than doctrinal clarity; empirical accounts should consider this practical role when drawing normative conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative benchmarking against other doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare eligibility metrics (affirmance, dissent, error rates) to metrics for other patent doctrines such as claim construction and obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benchmarking against other doctrines places eligibility predictability in context and avoids misleading claims that eligibility is uniquely unpredictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and data availability (use of open datasets)
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors used the Federal Circuit Dataset Project, an open-source dataset of all Federal Circuit decisions, and emphasize a commitment to transparency and data availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open data and reproducible methods are methodological standards for empirical work; they enable verification, extension, and benchmarking of findings about predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical coding methodology and reviewer procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: The study used human coding (three coders reviewed each of the 153 affirming opinions excluding Rule 36) to identify legal errors and classify dispositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigorous coding protocols (multiple coders, exclusion/inclusion rules, handling of summary dispositions) and reporting of coder procedures are essential for the credibility of empirical measures like error rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-learnability as evidence of doctrinal structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior work (e.g., training an AI classifier in 2018 based on USPTO eligibility decisions) suggests eligibility decisions can be predicted by algorithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrations that classifiers can learn patterns in eligibility decisions provide convergent evidence of predictability; however, they are sensitive to dataset composition (e.g., prevalence of certain case types).
